subtasks.title: Pin down the exact product facts that drive the legal analysis
subtasks.description:
The legal answer changes completely based on a few product details I have to assume rather than know. This subtask captures the assumptions I researched against, so the human can correct any that are wrong — a wrong assumption here invalidates whole sections of the report.

Assumptions used:
1. The face scan produces a biometric template/faceprint (mathematical representation), not just a stored photo. This matters: IL BIPA covers a "scan of face geometry"; a bare photograph is excluded.
2. Verification is 1:1 (selfie vs. government ID) not 1:N against a database.
3. A third-party vendor performs the matching (Persona / Jumio / Onfido / Socure / Veriff class of provider).
4. The scan and/or template is transmitted to that vendor.
5. Users are consumers acting in a personal capacity, not employees.
6. App is available nationwide with no state-level gating today.
7. No sale or trade of biometric data to third parties for consideration.
8. No use of the biometric data to train models.

If #1 is false (photo only, no geometry extraction) the BIPA exposure drops sharply. If #7 or #8 are false, the exposure rises sharply — BIPA bars profiting from biometric data outright, and model training is the current litigation frontier.

subtasks.title: Research Illinois BIPA — the statute that actually decides your launch map
subtasks.description:
Illinois 740 ILCS 14 (BIPA). FINDINGS — this is the state that decides the launch map.

COVERAGE: "Biometric identifier" expressly includes a "scan of hand or face geometry." Photographs are excluded from the definition of identifier, BUT "biometric information" separately covers any data *based on* an identifier used to identify a person, regardless of how captured or converted. So extracting a face template from an uploaded selfie is squarely in scope. Our flow is covered.

THE FIVE DUTIES (s.15):
- 15(a) — Written, PUBLICLY AVAILABLE policy with a retention schedule and destruction guidelines. Outer limit: destroy when the initial purpose is satisfied OR within 3 years of the individual's last interaction, whichever is FIRST. For identity verification the "initial purpose is satisfied" prong is the binding one — once the user is verified, the purpose is spent. Mora v. J&M Plating (2022 IL App (2d) 210692) held the policy must exist by the time you take possession; you cannot write it later.
- 15(b) — BEFORE collection: (1) written notice that biometrics are being collected/stored, (2) written notice of the specific purpose AND length of term, (3) a written release. 2024 amendment confirms electronic signature satisfies "written release."
- 15(c) — No selling, leasing, trading or otherwise profiting from biometric data. Flat prohibition, not consent-curable.
- 15(d) — No disclosure/redisclosure without separate consent. This is the one that catches the vendor hand-off.
- 15(e) — Reasonable standard of care in storage and transmission.

DAMAGES: $1,000 per negligent violation / $5,000 per reckless or intentional, whichever is greater than actual damages, PLUS attorneys' fees, costs, expert fees, and injunctive relief (s.20). Fee-shifting is what makes this economically attractive to the plaintiffs' bar.

PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION: Yes, and it is the only broad one in the country. Rosenbach v. Six Flags (2019 IL 123186) — a bare procedural violation makes you "aggrieved"; no actual injury required. This is the whole ballgame.

DAMAGES CAP (the 2024 reform): SB 2979 / Public Act 103-0769, effective 2 Aug 2024, overruled Cothron v. White Castle. Repeated collection of the same identifier from the same person by the same method = ONE violation, one recovery. Same for 15(d) disclosures to the same recipient. Practical effect: exposure is now ~$1k-$5k PER PERSON per violated subsection, not per scan.
- IMPORTANT UPDATE: Clay v. Union Pacific Railroad, No. 25-2185 (7th Cir. Apr. 1, 2026) held the amendment applies RETROACTIVELY to cases pending when it was enacted. The per-scan theory is dead.
- Do not over-read the cap. You can still be hit for a separate recovery per subsection violated (15(a), 15(b), 15(d), 15(e)), so a sloppy build is ~$4k-$20k per class member, and a 50,000-user Illinois class is still an existential number.

LIMITATIONS PERIOD: Tims v. Black Horse Carriers split it — 5 years for 15(a), 15(b), 15(e) claims; 1 year for 15(c)-(d) publication claims. Your notice/consent exposure looks back 5 years.

DIRECTLY ON-POINT CASE LINE — this is why I rate Illinois as the top risk. Selfie-plus-ID identity verification at signup is an actively litigated fact pattern, not a theoretical one:
- Davis v. Jumio Corp., No. 22-CV-00776 (N.D. Ill. Feb. 14, 2023) — user uploaded driver's licence photo then a selfie during Binance signup; Jumio scanned both to create and store a face template. Alleged failure to obtain written release and to give notice of use/retention/sharing/destruction. Motion to dismiss DENIED.
- Czyszczon v. Jumio (Phemex signup) — same pattern; additional allegation that the template should have been destroyed once verification completed but was retained instead. This is exactly the 15(a) "initial purpose satisfied" failure mode.
- Rivera / McGoveran v. Amazon Web Services — vendors held potentially liable; "we tried our best to comply" rejected as a defence.
TAKEAWAY: both we AND our IDV vendor are exposed, and the vendor being contractually responsible does not extinguish our own 15(b)/15(d) duties.

GLBA EXEMPTION — check but probably unavailable: s.25(c) says BIPA does not apply "in any manner" to a financial institution or affiliate subject to GLBA Title V. Courts have been hostile to stretching it: in Davis the court found insufficient evidence Binance qualified and doubted the exemption could shelter Jumio derivatively. A subscription consumer app is very unlikely to qualify. Do not build a compliance plan on this.

MASS ARBITRATION: BIPA became a staple of mass arbitration campaigns in 2025 and this continues into 2026. An arbitration clause with a class waiver is NOT a clean escape — it converts one class action into thousands of individual filings with per-case fees. See Wallrich v. Samsung (7th Cir.) on the fee-payment trap. Arbitration clause drafting is a real decision, not a formality.

subtasks.title: Research Texas CUBI and Washington HB 1493 — AG-enforced, high theoretical penalties
subtasks.description:
FINDINGS — Texas and Washington. Both AG-only, but they are NOT equivalent risks. Texas is now arguably scarier than Illinois in absolute dollars; Washington may not even apply to us.

=== TEXAS — CUBI, Tex. Bus. & Com. Code s.503.001 (in force since 2009) ===
COVERAGE: "Biometric identifier" = retina/iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or RECORD OF HAND OR FACE GEOMETRY. Note there is no photograph carve-out in the Texas definition (unlike Washington). Our face template is covered.

DUTIES:
- Inform the individual AND obtain consent BEFORE capture for a commercial purpose. Statute does not require the consent be written — informed consent suffices — but written is the safe build.
- No sale, lease or disclosure for a commercial purpose except narrow exceptions.
- Store/transmit/protect with reasonable care, at least as protective as how you treat your other confidential information.
- DESTROY within a reasonable time, and NOT LATER THAN THE FIRST ANNIVERSARY of the date the purpose for collecting expired. For signup IDV the purpose expires at verification, so the outer limit is ~1 year from verification — but "within a reasonable time" is the operative constraint and the AG reads it aggressively.

PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION: NONE. Texas AG has EXCLUSIVE enforcement authority.

PENALTY: up to $25,000 PER VIOLATION.

WHY TEXAS IS NOW A TOP-TIER THREAT DESPITE NO PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION — this is the counter-intuitive finding:
- The AG's position is that unlawful CAPTURE and unlawful STORAGE are SEPARATE violations. In the Meta complaint the AG argued that because collection was unlawful, retaining it for any length of time was also unlawful. Under that theory one bad capture is up to $50,000, not $25,000.
- The AG aggregates per-violation penalties across every affected resident. That arithmetic produced:
  * Meta / Facebook — $1.4 BILLION settlement, July 2024, over unlawful collection and use of facial recognition data. Largest settlement ever obtained by a single state in such an action.
  * Google — $1.375 BILLION settlement finalised May 2025, resolving claims including CUBI biometric claims (voiceprints and face geometry via Google Photos, Assistant, Nest Hub Max).
- Because the AG aggregates across millions of users, per-violation penalties can compound past anything BIPA's private bar has produced. Texas has been described in the practitioner press as the new leading privacy regulator, displacing California.
- Texas also filed CUBI actions as early as 2022 targeting AI training on biometric identifiers, so this is a sustained programme, not a one-off.
NET: no class action risk, but genuine bet-the-company regulator risk, and the enforcement appetite is demonstrated rather than theoretical.

=== WASHINGTON — RCW 19.375 (HB 1493, 2017) ===
DUTIES: May not ENROLL a biometric identifier in a database for a commercial purpose without first giving notice, obtaining consent, OR providing a mechanism to prevent subsequent commercial use. Note the three-way disjunctive path — more flexible than BIPA. Plus no sale/lease/disclosure without consent, reasonable security, and retention no longer than reasonably necessary for the purpose.
PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION: NONE. AG-only, via the Consumer Protection Act (RCW 19.86); violation is deemed an unfair or deceptive act. Civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation. Washington has generated far less litigation than Illinois precisely because individuals cannot sue under this chapter.

*** THE BIG WASHINGTON WRINKLE — RCW 19.375.010(1) may exclude us entirely ***
The definition expressly states that "biometric identifier" does NOT include "a physical or digital photograph, video or audio recording OR DATA GENERATED THEREFROM." Our flow generates a face template FROM a digital selfie photograph. On the plain text, a template derived from a photo is arguably outside RCW 19.375 altogether. This is the single most important state-level nuance I found, because it is the opposite of the Illinois position (where deriving a template from a photo pulls you IN via "biometric information"). Do not assume BIPA logic transfers. Worth a specific counsel sign-off — it could take Washington off the board for the biometric statute.

*** BUT — Washington My Health My Data Act (MHMDA, RCW 19.373) HAS A PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION ***
This is the trap that catches people who check RCW 19.375, find the photo exclusion, and relax.
- MHMDA lists biometric data within its very broad definition of "consumer health data," and it has NO photo carve-out.
- It provides a broad private right of action enforceable via the Washington CPA. First class action filed 10 Feb 2025, and it alleged precisely failure to obtain consent before collecting/sharing biometric data and failure to make the statutorily required clear and conspicuous consent disclosures.
- MITIGATING FACTORS, which are why I do not rank WA with Illinois: (1) the WA CPA has NO statutory damages — a plaintiff must prove causation and actual injury to "business or property," a real hurdle; (2) MHMDA's consent obligation is limited to collection/processing/sharing for SECONDARY purposes beyond what is necessary to provide the consumer-requested product or service. IDV at signup is plausibly necessary to provide the requested service, which is a strong argument against the core collection needing MHMDA consent.
- STILL REQUIRED regardless: a separate Consumer Health Data Privacy Policy, and honouring MHMDA access and deletion rights, which are broader than typical US privacy laws. Note the practical problem: deletion rights over biometric data have to be implemented without breaking reference templates and verification processes.
- OPEN QUESTION FOR COUNSEL: is a faceprint used purely for identity verification "consumer health data" at all, given MHMDA ties the concept to physical or mental health status? Arguable both ways. Unresolved.

subtasks.title: Research Colorado and California as the two 'sensitive data' regimes that behave differently from the rest
subtasks.description:
FINDINGS — Colorado and California. Both treat biometrics as sensitive data rather than via a standalone BIPA-style statute, but they behave very differently from each other and from the Tier 2 bloc.

=== COLORADO — CPA as amended by HB 24-1130, effective 1 JULY 2025 ===
*** THIS IS THE SLEEPER TRAP FOR A STARTUP. *** Signed 31 May 2024, adds s.6-1-1314 to the Colorado Privacy Act.

WHY IT'S A TRAP: the biometric provisions apply to ANY controller that controls or processes ANY AMOUNT of biometric data or identifiers, REGARDLESS of whether the controller meets the CPA's normal 100,000-consumer / 25,000-consumer-plus-revenue thresholds. Almost every other comprehensive state privacy law has a volume threshold that a pre-launch startup falls below. Colorado's biometric rules do not. If we process one Colorado resident's faceprint, we are in scope from day one. This is the most likely place for us to be accidentally non-compliant at launch.

DUTIES under s.6-1-1314:
- CONSENT before collection of a biometric identifier.
- A written policy, MADE PUBLICLY AVAILABLE, covering retention schedule, destruction guidelines, AND breach-response procedures. Note the breach-response element — this goes beyond BIPA s.15(a).
- No selling, leasing or trading biometric identifiers.
- Consumer right of ACCESS to their biometric data.
- Protections extended to employees (mostly irrelevant to us, though note employers may condition employment on biometric collection for limited purposes without prior consent).
- If collected from minors, HB 24-1130 stacks with SB 24-041 (effective 1 Oct 2025), including parental consent for under-13s.

ENFORCEMENT: Colorado AG AND district attorneys, under CPA s.6-1-112(1)(a). NO private right of action. Penalties up to $20,000 per violation. The CO AG finalised amended CPA rules in Dec 2024 addressing both HB 24-1130 and SB 24-041.

RISK RATING: high compliance-obligation risk, moderate consequence risk. It will not produce a class action, but it is the state most likely to catch us out because the thresholds don't protect us.

=== CALIFORNIA — CCPA/CPRA, no standalone biometric statute ===
THRESHOLD FIRST — we may be entirely out of scope at launch. CCPA applies to a for-profit doing business in CA that meets ANY of: (a) annual gross revenue over $26,625,000 for the 2026 compliance year (inflation-adjusted, was $25M); (b) buys/sells/shares personal information of 100,000+ California consumers or households; (c) derives 50%+ of annual revenue from selling/sharing personal information. A pre-launch subscription app likely meets NONE of these initially. CONTRAST WITH COLORADO — this is exactly why the two states need separate treatment.

IF/WHEN IN SCOPE:
- Biometric information is expressly SENSITIVE PERSONAL INFORMATION. Triggers: Notice at Collection before collecting (must state categories, purposes, retention period, and whether sold/shared), and the consumer's RIGHT TO LIMIT use and disclosure of sensitive PI. Note the CCPA model is opt-OUT/limit-based, not the opt-IN written release BIPA demands — a genuinely different architecture.
- Purpose limitation and data minimisation; service provider/contractor contract terms binding vendors to specified business purposes (relevant to the IDV vendor contract).

NEW AND IMPORTANT — CPPA regulations approved by the Office of Administrative Law 23 Sept 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026:
- RISK ASSESSMENTS (11 CCR s.7150(a)): a business must complete a risk assessment BEFORE initiating any processing involving "significant risk." "Processing sensitive personal information" is an express trigger — and biometric information is sensitive PI. SO: if we are CCPA-covered, our face-scan processing requires a documented risk assessment completed BEFORE we start processing. In effect as of 1 Jan 2026. Either the CPPA or the AG can demand a copy at any time and we must produce it within 30 days.
- Submission of risk assessments to the CPPA and ADMT pre-use notice obligations phase in from April 2027 / Dec 2027; cybersecurity audit obligations phase from April 2028 through April 2030 by revenue band (smallest businesses, under $50M, by 1 Apr 2030).
- ADMT: pre-use notice and opt-out apply where ADMT is used for "significant decisions." Access to a consumer subscription app is probably NOT a "significant decision" (that concept targets lending, housing, employment, healthcare, education), so I assess ADMT obligations as likely inapplicable — but worth counsel confirming, since a failed face match denies service.

PENALTIES: CPPA administrative fines, inflation-adjusted — approx $2,663 per unintentional violation and $7,988 per intentional violation or one involving a minor (2025 figures; the statutory base figures are $2,500/$7,500). The CA AG has concurrent authority. CPPA has been actively enforcing — 2025 saw a $632,500 fine against Honda and $345,178 against Todd Snyder, plus a Data Broker Enforcement Strike Force. None were biometric-specific but the appetite is demonstrated.

PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION — BREACH ONLY, and biometrics are in scope: Cal. Civ. Code s.1798.150 gives a private right of action where a defined category of unencrypted/unredacted personal information is exposed by a failure to maintain reasonable security. Biometric data is within the qualifying categories. Statutory damages $100-$750 per consumer per incident, or actual damages if greater. So California exposure is not zero — it is contingent on a security incident. A breach of a faceprint database is our worst-case California scenario, and it converts a regulatory matter into a class action.
ALSO: plaintiffs routinely bootstrap CCPA violations into California UCL (s.17200) "unlawful prong" claims to get around the breach-only limitation — see the Clearview-related Burke v. Clearview AI UCL claim predicated on CCPA violations. Treat the "no PRA outside breach" comfort as partial.

subtasks.title: Establish the consent + notice + retention obligations as one merged operational spec
subtasks.description:
FINDINGS — the merged build spec. Derived by taking the strictest requirement on each dimension across all states, so one build clears the whole country. Build to Illinois + Colorado and you are over-compliant nearly everywhere else.

--- 1. THE CONSENT GATE (hardest requirement: Illinois s.15(b)) ---
Must be a SEPARATE, AFFIRMATIVE, PRE-COLLECTION act. Specifically:
- Presented BEFORE the camera activates. Not after capture, not during processing. "Prior to collection" is the statutory language and courts read it literally.
- A DISTINCT checkbox or signature step. NOT bundled into acceptance of the Terms of Service or Privacy Policy. Consent buried in a ToS scroll is the single most common BIPA failure and is what plaintiffs plead first. Do not accept "user agreed to our Terms" as consent.
- Unchecked by default. No pre-ticked boxes, no "by continuing you agree."
- Electronic signature is FINE — the 2024 BIPA amendment expressly confirms e-signature satisfies "written release." A tap-to-accept with a logged record is sufficient. You do not need a wet signature.
- MUST BE LOGGED per user with timestamp, the exact notice version shown, and the consent artifact. If you cannot produce, for any individual user, the precise screen they saw and when, you cannot defend the claim. Version the notice text and retain old versions forever.
- Separate consent for the VENDOR DISCLOSURE (BIPA s.15(d)). Consent to collect is not consent to transmit to a third-party processor. Name the vendor or at minimum the category, in the consent.

--- 2. THE NOTICE CONTENT (union of all state requirements) ---
The pre-collection notice must state, in plain language:
(a) That a biometric identifier / face geometry scan is being collected and stored — use the word "biometric," don't euphemise it as "photo check";
(b) The SPECIFIC PURPOSE — identity verification at account opening;
(c) The SPECIFIC LENGTH OF TERM for which it will be collected, stored and used — an actual duration, not "as long as necessary." Illinois s.15(b)(2) requires the term be stated. This is a frequently pleaded defect;
(d) That it will be disclosed to a named third-party verification provider;
(e) How to withdraw consent and the consequence of doing so;
(f) For California (if in scope): a compliant Notice at Collection including categories, purposes, retention period, and whether sold/shared;
(g) For Washington (if MHMDA applies): categories collected/shared, purpose, categories of recipients, and instructions for withdrawing consent — these four items were the exact pleading in the first MHMDA class action.

--- 3. THE PUBLIC RETENTION POLICY (Illinois s.15(a) + Colorado s.6-1-1314) ---
- Must be WRITTEN and PUBLICLY AVAILABLE — a real URL, publicly reachable, not inside the app or behind login.
- Must exist BEFORE first possession of any biometric data. Mora v. J&M Plating: you cannot draft it retroactively. Ship the policy before you ship the feature.
- Must contain: a retention SCHEDULE, and GUIDELINES for permanent destruction.
- Colorado additionally requires a PROTOCOL FOR RESPONDING TO A DATA SECURITY INCIDENT affecting biometric data. BIPA does not require this, so Colorado sets the ceiling here — include it.

--- 4. RETENTION LIMIT — the strictest rule wins, and it is very short ---
Governing constraint: Illinois s.15(a) — destroy when the INITIAL PURPOSE IS SATISFIED, or within 3 YEARS of the individual's last interaction, WHICHEVER IS FIRST.
*** For identity verification at signup, the initial purpose is satisfied THE MOMENT VERIFICATION COMPLETES. The 3-year outer bound is a red herring for us — it never becomes the operative limit. ***
Texas: destroy within a reasonable time, no later than the first anniversary of the date the collection purpose expires.
=> RECOMMENDED BUILD: delete the face template and the source selfie within 24-48 HOURS of the verification decision, and retain only (i) a non-biometric boolean "verified" flag, (ii) the verification timestamp, (iii) an audit reference ID, and (iv) the consent record. Immediate deletion is the single highest-leverage design decision available to us — see below.
The Czyszczon v. Jumio complaint alleged exactly this failure: the template should have been destroyed once identity was verified but was retained instead. Do not repeat it.
CAVEAT TO RESOLVE: if the product wants the faceprint for later re-authentication or account recovery, the purpose does NOT expire at signup and this whole analysis changes — retention becomes ongoing and the risk profile rises sharply. This is a product decision, not a legal one. Escalated as a human subtask.

--- 5. THE STRATEGIC POINT: DON'T RETAIN, AND PREFERABLY DON'T POSSESS ---
Most obligations attach to COLLECTING or POSSESSING biometric data. Two architectural moves materially shrink the legal surface:
(a) Zero-retention / ephemeral matching — template created, matched, destroyed in-session, never persisted. Kills the s.15(a) retention claims and most of the Texas storage-as-separate-violation theory.
(b) On-device matching where feasible — if the template never leaves the handset and we never possess it, s.15(d) disclosure duties and much of the vendor-liability chain fall away.
Neither eliminates the s.15(b) notice-and-consent duty. Consent is required for the CAPTURE regardless of what you do afterwards. There is no architecture that avoids the consent gate.
NOTE: vendors market "zero-data architecture" for exactly this reason. Verify the claim contractually and technically — the vendor's marketing page is not a defence.

--- 6. SECURITY (BIPA s.15(e), CUBI, RCW 19.375, CCPA) ---
Reasonable care, and at least as protective as how we treat our other confidential information (Texas's explicit standard). Encrypt at rest and in transit. This is also the CCPA breach-PRA exposure point ($100-$750 per consumer per incident) — a faceprint breach is the one scenario that creates a California class action, and it is the reason (5) matters so much. Data you already deleted cannot be breached.

--- 7. THINGS TO NEVER DO (flat prohibitions, not consent-curable) ---
- Do NOT sell, lease, trade or otherwise profit from biometric data. Prohibited outright in IL s.15(c), TX, WA, CO, and NYC. Consent does not cure this.
- Do NOT use the scans to train or improve any model, ours or a vendor's. This is the current litigation frontier — May 2026 BIPA cases targeting voiceprint extraction for AI training are being read as a new and easier route to class-wide claims, and Texas has been bringing CUBI actions over AI training on biometric identifiers since 2022. Check the IDV vendor's contract for a training/improvement licence and strike it.
- Do NOT let the vendor retain beyond our own retention window. Flow the deletion obligation through contractually with an audit right.

subtasks.title: Classify all 50 states + DC into risk tiers and produce the disposition table
subtasks.description:
FINDINGS — all 50 states + DC classified. Full accounting = 51 jurisdictions: 4 in Tier 1, 19 in Tier 2, 28 in Tier 3. Full table with per-state detail is in the attached report on the parent task; this is the classification and the reasoning.

=== TIER 1 — BIOMETRIC-SPECIFIC DUTIES (4 jurisdictions) ===
Illinois, Texas, Washington, Colorado.
Only THREE states have a dedicated standalone biometric statute as of 2026: IL (BIPA), TX (CUBI), WA (RCW 19.375 + MHMDA). Colorado is the fourth Tier 1 member because HB 24-1130 grafted biometric-specific duties onto the CPA effective 1 July 2025. See the three dedicated Tier 1 subtasks for full detail on each.
KEY POINT: no new dedicated state biometric statute was enacted in 2025. New York's BIPA-clone (S1422, Liu) has been introduced and re-introduced but is STILL PENDING, not law. Arkansas tried and failed — SB 258 (2025) originally had biometric consent provisions but the Senate committee stripped all biometric and AI sections before passage. So the Tier 1 list has been stable, but NY is the obvious watch item: if NY passes a BIPA clone with a private right of action, our risk map changes overnight and NY is a much bigger market than Illinois.

=== TIER 2 — COMPREHENSIVE PRIVACY LAW, BIOMETRICS AS "SENSITIVE DATA" (19) ===
Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia.
(Plus Colorado and Texas, counted in Tier 1 — so 21 states total have a comprehensive privacy law in force. Published counts say "20 states" because most lists omit Arkansas, whose APDPA is narrower; I include it because it does classify biometric data used for identification as sensitive data.)

THE COMMON PATTERN — this is why they can be treated as a bloc:
- Biometric data is SENSITIVE DATA, requiring OPT-IN CONSENT before processing. Utah is the outlier: it requires notice-and-opportunity-to-opt-out rather than opt-in.
- A DATA PROTECTION ASSESSMENT is required for processing sensitive data. This is a real deliverable — a written document — and it's the most commonly skipped obligation.
- Consumer rights: access, delete, correct, portability, opt out of sale/targeted advertising.
- NO PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION in any of them. AG-enforced only.
- Penalties: modal figure is $7,500 per violation. Outliers: Florida $50,000 (highest of any state law, but see thresholds); Rhode Island, Delaware, New Hampshire, Maryland, Arkansas ~$10,000; California $2,663 unintentional / $7,988 intentional (inflation-adjusted).
- Most have a cure period, though several have removed or sunset theirs (Arkansas's 60-day cure expires 1 Jan 2027).

*** THRESHOLDS ARE THE DECISIVE ISSUE IN TIER 2 — most of these will NOT apply to us at launch ***
Typical threshold is 100,000 state residents, which a pre-launch app is nowhere near. Practical effect: most of Tier 2 is dormant for us initially and switches on as we scale. Note the exceptions:
- TEXAS TDPSA — NO revenue and NO volume threshold. Applies to anyone conducting business in Texas or serving Texas residents. Only escape is the SBA small-business exemption (industry-specific; broadly <500 employees or under ~$7M average receipts). So Texas hits us TWICE — CUBI regardless of size, plus TDPSA once we outgrow SBA small-business status. Reinforces Texas as the top-priority state.
- NEBRASKA — same SBA small-business model as Texas.
- RHODE ISLAND — notably low threshold (35,000 residents) and NO cure period.
- FLORIDA — effectively inapplicable; the FDBR is limited to businesses over $1 BILLION in revenue. Its $50,000 penalty is scary-looking and irrelevant to us. Do not waste time here.
- COLORADO — biometric provisions have NO threshold at all (Tier 1, see that subtask).
=> ACTION: threshold analysis is not a one-time exercise. Obligations switch on as user counts cross state lines. Needs a recurring review, created as a human subtask.

*** MARYLAND IS THE STRICTEST TIER 2 STATE AND DESERVES SEPARATE ATTENTION ***
MODPA (effective Oct 2025) departs from the bloc in ways that matter to us:
- Collection/processing/sharing of sensitive data is BANNED unless STRICTLY NECESSARY to provide or maintain a product or service the consumer requested. This is a necessity standard, not a consent standard — consent does NOT cure it. Identity verification at signup is defensible as strictly necessary, but we must document that necessity assessment.
- Outright prohibition on the SALE of sensitive data, with consent expressly unable to override. First of its kind.
- MODPA classifies biometric data as sensitive REGARDLESS of how it is used, whereas most states only do so when used for identification. Broader hook than the rest of the bloc.
- No sale/targeted advertising involving personal data of anyone under 18.

=== TIER 3 — NO BIOMETRIC CONSENT DUTY (28 jurisdictions) ===
Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, DC, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Vermont, West Virginia, Wisconsin, Wyoming.
WHAT APPLIES: no biometric-specific notice or consent obligation. Exposure is limited to (a) data-breach notification statutes — most of these states include biometric data in the definition of protected personal information, so a faceprint breach triggers notification duties; (b) general UDAP/deceptive-trade-practices statutes, which bite only if our public privacy representations are false; (c) reasonable-security requirements in some states.
BOTTOM LINE FOR TIER 3: the compliance ask is "don't lie in your privacy policy, secure the data, and be ready to notify on breach." No consent gate legally required. If we build the Illinois-grade flow nationwide (recommended), we are far over-compliant here.

TIER 3 STATES WITH SPECIFIC FEATURES WORTH KNOWING:
- NEW YORK — the one to watch. No comprehensive law and no biometric statute, BUT: (i) the SHIELD Act imposes reasonable-security duties and includes biometric data in its breach definition; (ii) NYC Local Law 3 (NYC Admin Code ss.22-1201-1205, effective July 2021) HAS A PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION — see below; (iii) a BIPA-clone bill is pending. Note NY's Health Information Privacy Act did NOT advance.
- NEVADA — has a consumer health data law (SB 370) modelled on Washington's MHMDA. Worth a look if the MHMDA analysis concludes our faceprint is "consumer health data," since the same reasoning would travel.

=== LOCAL ORDINANCES — TWO CITIES HAVE PRIVATE RIGHTS OF ACTION, WHICH THEIR STATES DO NOT ===
This is the trap in relying on a state-level-only analysis. Both sit in states I classified as Tier 3 / Tier 2 respectively.
1. NEW YORK CITY — NYC Admin Code ss.22-1201-1205. Two duties: conspicuous SIGNAGE near customer entrances for "commercial establishments" that collect biometric identifier information, and a BLANKET BAN on selling, leasing, trading, sharing for value, or otherwise profiting from biometric identifier information. There IS a private right of action for persons "aggrieved."
   OUR LIKELY POSITION: probably NOT covered by the signage duty. "Commercial establishment" is defined as places of entertainment, retail stores, and food-and-drink establishments, and the notice mechanism is physical signage at customer entrances — the statute is premises-oriented and a mobile app has no entrance. The sale prohibition is drafted more broadly ("any person or entity") so we should treat the no-sale rule as applying to us regardless. Since we should never sell biometric data anyway, this costs us nothing.
2. PORTLAND, OREGON — City Code Chapter 34.10. Bans PRIVATE ENTITIES from using face recognition technologies in "places of public accommodation" in Portland. PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION: actual damages OR $1,000 PER DAY of violation, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees (subject to a 30-day pre-suit written demand requirement).
   OUR LIKELY POSITION: GENUINELY UNCERTAIN AND THIS ONE NEEDS COUNSEL. The ordinance has three exceptions and none clearly covers us — the user-verification exception is limited to accessing "the user's own personal or employer-issued communication and electronic devices," i.e. device unlock, NOT verifying identity to a service provider. So our escape route is arguing a mobile app is not a "place of public accommodation." That is contestable, and $1,000 per day of violation with fee-shifting is not a rounding error. Perkins Coie has described this as the country's strictest facial recognition law. FLAGGED AS A HUMAN SUBTASK.
Other cities (e.g. Baltimore) have enacted face-recognition restrictions; a full municipal sweep is out of scope here and noted as a residual risk.

subtasks.title: Name the genuinely dangerous states and say why, separating litigation risk from regulatory risk
subtasks.description:
FINDINGS — the ranked danger list. The brief asked which states are "genuinely dangerous." The critical move is separating TWO different risks that get conflated, because they call for different mitigations:
- LITIGATION RISK = can private plaintiffs and their lawyers sue us, ideally as a class, with statutory damages and fee-shifting? This is what kills startups, because it arrives unannounced and costs money to defend even when you win.
- REGULATORY RISK = can a state AG investigate and fine us? Slower, usually preceded by contact, often has a cure period, but the ceiling is much higher.
A state can have a strict statute and still be practically safe if nobody can sue. Conversely a state with modest penalties is dangerous if it has a private right of action. Strictness and danger are NOT the same axis.

=== RANK 1: ILLINOIS — the only true "consider not launching" state ===
Risk type: LITIGATION. Severity: extreme.
Why: the only broad private right of action for biometrics in the country. $1,000 negligent / $5,000 reckless per person, PLUS attorneys' fees — the fee-shifting is what creates a standing industry of plaintiffs' firms. Rosenbach means NO ACTUAL HARM IS NEEDED; a purely technical notice defect is actionable. Five-year lookback on the notice/consent claims. Over $1.5 billion in BIPA settlements since 2008.
Why it is specifically dangerous FOR US: selfie-plus-ID verification at signup is an actively litigated fact pattern, not a hypothetical — Davis v. Jumio and Czyszczon v. Jumio are our exact flow, and both survived motions to dismiss. Plaintiffs' firms already know this template and are actively recruiting.
Mitigating factors that lower this from "catastrophic" to "serious": the 2024 amendment (SB 2979) killed per-scan damages, and Clay v. Union Pacific (7th Cir., 1 Apr 2026) confirmed it applies retroactively. Exposure is now roughly per-person-per-subsection rather than per-scan.
Honest sizing: a compliant build makes Illinois genuinely manageable. A non-compliant build with 50,000 Illinois users is roughly $50M-$250M of theoretical exposure before you argue about it. The variance between those two outcomes is entirely in the consent screen.
VERDICT: launch in Illinois ONLY with the full Illinois-grade flow verified by counsel. This is not a state to launch into "and fix later." Geofencing Illinois is a legitimate option if the consent flow will not be ready.

=== RANK 2: TEXAS — the biggest absolute numbers in the country ===
Risk type: REGULATORY (no private right of action at all). Severity: extreme ceiling, low probability for a small company.
Why: the Texas AG has secured the two largest biometric/privacy recoveries in US history — $1.4B from Meta (July 2024) and $1.375B from Google (finalised May 2025). Up to $25,000 per violation, and the AG's theory is that unlawful CAPTURE and unlawful STORAGE are separate violations, so one bad capture can be $50,000. The AG aggregates across every affected resident, which is how per-violation caps compound past anything the Illinois plaintiffs' bar has produced.
Also: CUBI has no size threshold, and the TDPSA has no revenue or volume threshold either (only the SBA small-business exemption). Texas is the hardest state to be accidentally out of scope in. Practitioners now describe Texas, not California, as the leading US privacy regulator.
Honest sizing: the AG hunts headline defendants. A pre-launch startup is not the target profile. But there is no cure-period safety net comparable to a class action's procedural runway, and the ceiling is company-ending.
VERDICT: fully compliant at launch. Cheap to do — Texas's requirements are a subset of Illinois's. Do not skip it because "no one can sue us."

=== RANK 3: COLORADO — the most likely place to be accidentally non-compliant ===
Risk type: REGULATORY. Severity: moderate ($20,000/violation, AG and district attorneys, no PRA).
Why it makes the danger list despite modest penalties: HB 24-1130's biometric provisions apply to any controller processing ANY AMOUNT of biometric data, REGARDLESS of the CPA's usual thresholds. Every other comprehensive-law state's threshold protects a pre-launch startup. Colorado's does not. It also demands something BIPA doesn't — a breach-response protocol inside the public retention policy. Effective 1 July 2025, so it is live now.
VERDICT: this is where an unprepared launch gets caught first. Highest ratio of "likely to be violated" to "expected to be checked."

=== RANK 4: WASHINGTON — dangerous only through a side door ===
Risk type: LITIGATION, but weak. Severity: moderate and uncertain.
RCW 19.375 is AG-only ($7,500/violation) and may not even reach us — its definition of "biometric identifier" EXPRESSLY EXCLUDES a digital photograph "or data generated therefrom," and our template is generated from a selfie. Plausibly out of scope entirely, which is the opposite of the Illinois result.
The real Washington risk is MHMDA (RCW 19.373), which HAS a broad private right of action via the state Consumer Protection Act, no photo carve-out, and the first class action (Feb 2025) pleaded exactly failure to obtain consent before collecting biometric data. WHY IT'S RANK 4 NOT RANK 2: the WA CPA has NO statutory damages — plaintiffs must prove causation and actual injury to business or property, a serious hurdle — and MHMDA's consent duty is limited to SECONDARY purposes beyond providing the consumer-requested service, which signup IDV arguably is not.
VERDICT: watch, don't panic. Two unresolved questions for counsel (photo carve-out; whether an IDV faceprint is "consumer health data" at all).

=== RANK 5: PORTLAND, OREGON — a city, not a state, and the sleeper on this list ===
Risk type: LITIGATION. Severity: uncertain but non-trivial.
$1,000 PER DAY of violation plus attorney's fees, with a private right of action, for private entities using face recognition in "places of public accommodation." The user-verification exception covers device unlock, NOT verifying identity to a service provider, so our only defence is that a mobile app isn't a place of public accommodation — contestable. Called the country's strictest facial recognition law.
VERDICT: genuinely unresolved. Get a specific opinion. Do not let this be discovered post-launch.

=== RANK 6: CALIFORNIA — dangerous ONLY if we have a breach ===
Risk type: mostly REGULATORY; LITIGATION only on breach.
We may be out of scope entirely at launch (thresholds: >$26.625M revenue for 2026, or 100,000+ CA consumers, or 50%+ revenue from selling PI). If in scope: notice at collection, right to limit sensitive PI, and a mandatory risk assessment BEFORE processing sensitive PI under 11 CCR s.7150(a), in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
The teeth: Cal. Civ. Code s.1798.150 gives a private right of action for a breach of unencrypted personal information — and biometric data qualifies — at $100-$750 per consumer per incident. A faceprint database breach is the single scenario that turns California into a class action. This is the strongest argument for the delete-immediately architecture: data we don't hold can't be breached.

=== NOT DANGEROUS, DESPITE APPEARANCES ===
- FLORIDA: $50,000 per violation is the highest state penalty in the country and is IRRELEVANT to us — the FDBR only applies to businesses with over $1 billion in revenue. Don't spend time here.
- The other ~17 Tier 2 states: opt-in consent for sensitive data, AG-only, no private right of action, and thresholds (typically 100,000 residents) that we don't meet at launch. Real obligations, low danger, and they switch on as we scale.
- The 28 Tier 3 states: no biometric consent duty at all. Breach notification and "don't lie in your privacy policy" only.

=== THE BOTTOM LINE ON "WHERE IS IT DANGEROUS TO LAUNCH" ===
There is exactly ONE state where the honest answer might be "don't launch yet": ILLINOIS, and only if the consent flow isn't ready.
Everywhere else the answer is "launch, but build it properly" — because the cost of building the Illinois-grade flow nationwide is a single well-designed consent screen plus a published retention policy plus aggressive deletion, and that same build over-satisfies all 50 states. GEOGRAPHIC GATING IS ALMOST CERTAINLY THE WRONG STRATEGY: it is more engineering work than just complying, it fails the moment someone travels or uses a VPN, and residency is genuinely hard to determine reliably. Compliance is cheaper than geofencing here. The one exception is using an Illinois geofence as a temporary safety valve if you must ship before the consent flow is signed off.

subtasks.title: Flag the non-biometric laws that hit at the same launch moment
subtasks.description:
FINDINGS — non-biometric laws that land at the same launch moment. Not in the original brief, but directly triggered by "consumer mobile app" + "monthly subscription" + "scans a user's face." Two of these three are arguably more likely to produce an enforcement contact at launch than the biometric statutes.

=== A. SUBSCRIPTION AUTO-RENEWAL — you charge monthly, so this applies in every state ===
FEDERAL STATUS — READ THIS BEFORE ANYONE BUILDS TO THE OLD ADVICE:
The FTC's "click-to-cancel" Negative Option Rule was VACATED IN ITS ENTIRETY by the Eighth Circuit on 8 July 2025 (Custom Communications, Inc. v. FTC), on procedural grounds — the FTC failed to conduct the required preliminary regulatory analysis. It was struck down days before its main disclosure, consent and cancellation provisions were to take effect on 14 July 2025. Much of the compliance content written in 2024-25 is now WRONG. Verify the date on any checklist someone hands you.
WHAT SURVIVES, AND IT IS PLENTY:
- ROSCA (Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act) — similar but less prescriptive disclosure, consent and cancellation duties. The FTC's interpretation of ROSCA is that cancellation must be at least as easy as the method used to sign up. Actively enforced.
- FTC Act s.5 and state UDAP statutes.
- The FTC has RESTARTED negative-option rulemaking, now following Magnuson-Moss procedures. Expect a replacement rule. Treat click-to-cancel as the design target regardless of the vacatur.
- State auto-renewal laws are untouched by the vacatur and are the real operative constraint.

CALIFORNIA ARL — the strictest, and the one to build to. Amended by AB 2863 (signed 24 Sept 2024), amendments EFFECTIVE 1 JULY 2025:
- Now expressly covers FREE TRIALS / "free-to-pay conversions" within "automatic renewal" and "continuous service."
- Strengthened affirmative consent requirements; anti-dark-pattern rules; prohibits confirming billing info as a substitute for consent.
- RETENTION OF PROOF OF CONSENT: must retain verification of the consumer's affirmative consent for a MINIMUM OF 3 YEARS, or 1 year following contract termination, whichever is LONGER.
  *** DIRECT CONFLICT TO MANAGE: the biometric analysis says destroy the face data almost immediately; the ARL says retain the subscription consent record for 3+ years. These are DIFFERENT records and must be stored separately. Do not let an engineer implement "delete the signup record" and wipe the ARL evidence, and do not let "retain consent proof for 3 years" become a reason to keep the faceprint. Two separate retention rules, two separate stores. This is the single most likely place for the two workstreams to collide badly.
- ANNUAL REMINDER: renewal frequency, amount charged, and clear cancellation instructions.
- MATCHING CANCELLATION CHANNEL: cancellation must be available through the same channel used to sign up, plus a click-to-cancel button for online signups; no obstructing or delaying cancellation.
RISK NOTE: California's ARL is enforced by the AG and district attorneys AND is a favourite hook for UCL class actions. For a consumer subscription app this is a higher-probability claim than a biometric claim in most states.

=== B. AGE / MINORS — the face scan makes this worse, not better ===
The general problem: once you scan a face at signup you have a strong basis to estimate age, which makes "we had no actual knowledge any users were minors" much harder to say. Face-based age assurance can convert a defence into an admission. Whether we run age estimation at all is a deliberate decision, not a default.

*** THE BIG ONE — STATE APP STORE ACCOUNTABILITY ACTS. These impose duties on DEVELOPERS, not just app stores. ***
- TEXAS App Store Accountability Act (SB 2420, signed 27 May 2025) — EFFECTIVE 1 JANUARY 2026 and IN FORCE: a preliminary injunction was STAYED by the Fifth Circuit (Nov 2025), so the law took effect. Requires app stores to verify ages at account creation and obtain parental consent for minors' downloads and in-app purchases, and to share age and consent signals with developers. Developer-side duties: receive and confirm the age/consent information, use it only for compliance purposes, transmit it securely with industry-standard encryption, and DELETE IT AFTER USE (Texas-specific).
- UTAH (enacted March 2025) and LOUISIANA (HB 570, signed 30 June 2025) have their own versions. More than a dozen other states are considering similar bills.
- These laws effectively impose a duty to verify the age of ALL users REGARDLESS of whether the app is aimed at minors. A general-audience subscription app is squarely in scope.
- Limited good-faith protection for developers relying on app-store-supplied age/consent data, but NO broad safe harbour for our own implementation mistakes.
- TENSION WORTH NAMING: these acts require collecting and confirming MORE personal data for age verification, which cuts directly against the data-minimisation duties in MODPA, the CPA and the CCPA. There is no clean answer; document the reasoning.
- *** STALENESS WARNING: enforcement timelines and liability frameworks for the Utah, Texas and Louisiana ASAAs SHIFTED during 2026 because of later legislation and court rulings. There is a June 2026 update tracking current status. This is fast-moving; re-verify the current position before relying on any of the above dates. Created as a human subtask. ***
OTHER MINORS ITEMS:
- COLORADO SB 24-041 (effective 1 Oct 2025) stacks with HB 24-1130 — if biometrics are collected from minors, both apply, including parental consent for under-13s.
- MARYLAND MODPA bans sale/targeted advertising of under-18s' personal data and treats a known under-13's data as sensitive automatically.
- ARKANSAS HB 1717 (Arkansas Online Privacy Act) — EFFECTIVE 1 JULY 2026, now live. COPPA-style but extends beyond it: applies to operators "directed at" children or with actual knowledge they are collecting from children OR TEENS (13-16), requiring consent from the teen or a parent before collecting personal information, and barring targeted advertising to them.
- CONNECTICUT and ARKANSAS both tightened minors' protections with age-appropriate design code requirements taking effect in 2026; more measures land in 2027.
- Federal COPPA still applies to under-13s independently.

=== C. RESIDUAL ITEMS I DID NOT RESEARCH — flagged so they aren't mistaken for cleared ===
- Biometric data is included in the definition of protected personal information in most state DATA BREACH NOTIFICATION statutes, including in Tier 3 states with no other biometric duty. A faceprint breach = 50-state notification analysis. Not researched state by state here.
- Illinois has separate AI-related statutes (e.g. the AI Video Interview Act) that don't apply to this flow but are adjacent if the product scope grows.
- A full municipal ordinance sweep beyond NYC and Portland was not done. Baltimore and others have face-recognition restrictions.
- GLBA/BSA/KYC: if the subscription is ever bundled with anything financial, the analysis changes materially — and possibly favourably, given BIPA's GLBA exemption.

subtasks.title: DECIDE: is the faceprint deleted after verification, or kept for re-authentication?
subtasks.description:
BLOCKING DECISION — this one answer changes the entire risk profile and several other subtasks depend on it. Nothing else should be built until it's settled.

OPTION A — delete template + source selfie within 24-48h of the verification decision, keep only a 'verified' boolean, timestamp, audit ID and the consent record.
  * Illinois s.15(a) retention claims largely disappear (initial purpose satisfied = destroy).
  * Kills most of the Texas AG's 'storage is a separate violation' theory.
  * Removes the California breach-PRA exposure ($100-$750/consumer) because there is no faceprint to breach.
  * Cost: no biometric re-auth, no biometric account recovery. Returning users re-verify from scratch if ever needed.

OPTION B — retain the template for ongoing re-authentication or account recovery.
  * The 'initial purpose' never expires, so the 3-year-from-last-interaction clock becomes the operative limit instead of immediate deletion.
  * Creates a standing biometric database: permanent breach exposure, ongoing BIPA s.15(a)/(e) duties, deletion-request engineering under Colorado access rights and Washington MHMDA, and a materially bigger Texas storage-theory footprint.
  * Needs a much stronger security posture and probably a higher insurance limit.

RECOMMENDATION: Option A unless there is a concrete product requirement for biometric re-auth. The legal cost of Option B is large and the product benefit is often assumed rather than real.

Write the decision into this task's description when made, then confirm the answer to the person building the consent screen and retention policy.

subtasks.title: Confirm or correct the 8 product assumptions the whole analysis rests on
subtasks.description:
The research assumed 8 facts (full list in the completed subtask 'Pin down the exact product facts that drive the legal analysis'). Read them and correct any that are wrong, because several would invalidate whole sections.

The three that matter most:
1. Does the flow actually extract a face TEMPLATE / geometry (vs. just storing a photo or having a human review it)? If no geometry is ever extracted, Illinois BIPA exposure drops sharply.
2. Do we, or the vendor, use the scans to TRAIN or IMPROVE any model? If yes, risk rises sharply — this is the active litigation frontier (May 2026 BIPA voiceprint/AI-training cases; Texas has brought CUBI actions over AI training since 2022). Check the vendor contract for a training or 'service improvement' licence.
3. Do we sell, licence, or share biometric data for anything of value? If yes, this is a flat prohibition in IL/TX/WA/CO/NYC that CONSENT CANNOT CURE. Must stop before launch.

Also confirm: 1:1 verification (not 1:N database search), which vendor, whether users can be under 18, and whether the subscription is ever bundled with a financial product (which could open the BIPA GLBA exemption).

subtasks.title: Get outside counsel to answer the 4 specific open questions I could not resolve
subtasks.description:
These are genuine unresolved legal questions, not things I skipped. Send them as a discrete list — this should be a short, cheap engagement, not an open-ended 50-state survey, because the 50-state work is already done and attached to the parent task.

Q1. PORTLAND, OREGON (highest priority — has a private right of action). Portland City Code ch. 34.10 bans private entities using face recognition in 'places of public accommodation'; damages are actual OR $1,000 PER DAY of violation, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees, subject to a 30-day pre-suit written demand. Is a consumer mobile app a 'place of public accommodation' for these purposes? Note the user-verification exception only covers accessing the user's OWN personal or employer-issued devices, so it does NOT appear to cover verifying identity to a service provider. If we are covered, we need a Portland answer before launch.

Q2. WASHINGTON, two parts. (a) RCW 19.375.010(1) excludes from 'biometric identifier' any 'physical or digital photograph, video or audio recording OR DATA GENERATED THEREFROM.' Our template is generated from a digital selfie. Does that put us outside RCW 19.375 entirely? (b) If so, does the My Health My Data Act (RCW 19.373) still reach us — i.e. is a faceprint used purely for identity verification 'consumer health data' when MHMDA ties the concept to physical or mental health status? MHMDA matters because it HAS a private right of action via the WA Consumer Protection Act.

Q3. Is the 'initial purpose' under BIPA s.15(a) satisfied at the moment of successful verification, such that immediate deletion is required? Confirm our proposed 24-48h deletion window is defensible as 'when the initial purpose has been satisfied' and not merely convenient.

Q4. Review the actual consent screen copy and the published retention policy before launch. This is the single highest-leverage review — the difference between a defensible Illinois position and a $5,000-per-person one is the wording and placement of this screen.

BRIEF THEM ON THE FACT PATTERN: selfie + government ID, 1:1 match, third-party vendor, consumer subscription app. Point them at Davis v. Jumio, No. 22-CV-00776 (N.D. Ill. Feb. 14, 2023) and the Czyszczon v. Jumio complaint as the closest analogues.

subtasks.title: DECIDE Illinois launch posture: full compliant flow, or geofence IL until the flow is signed off
subtasks.description:
The only state where 'maybe don't launch yet' is a real answer. Decide explicitly rather than by default.

THE NUMBERS: $1,000 negligent / $5,000 reckless PER PERSON, per violated subsection, plus attorneys' fees. No actual harm needed (Rosenbach v. Six Flags). Five-year lookback on the s.15(a)/(b)/(e) claims. Our exact fact pattern (selfie + ID at signup via a third-party vendor) has already survived motions to dismiss twice against Jumio.
GOOD NEWS: the 2024 amendment killed per-scan damages and Clay v. Union Pacific (7th Cir., 1 Apr 2026) made that retroactive, so exposure is per-person, not per-scan.

OPTION 1 (RECOMMENDED): launch in Illinois with the full compliant flow, counsel-reviewed. The build is ONE well-designed consent screen + a published retention policy + aggressive deletion. It is genuinely cheap relative to the exposure, and the same build over-satisfies all 50 states.
OPTION 2: geofence Illinois temporarily if the consent flow will not be ready and counsel-reviewed by launch. Use as a safety valve only.
DO NOT choose a permanent 50-state geographic gating strategy: it is more engineering work than complying, it breaks with travel and VPNs, residency is unreliable to determine, and it leaves you non-compliant anyway for misclassified users.

Depends on: the counsel review and the retention decision. Record the decision here.

subtasks.title: Draft the pre-collection biometric consent screen copy and the public retention policy
subtasks.description:
Two deliverables to draft, then send to counsel as Q4 of the counsel review. Full spec is in the completed subtask 'Establish the consent + notice + retention obligations as one merged operational spec' — build to that spec, which is the strictest-common-denominator across all 50 states.

DELIVERABLE 1 — CONSENT SCREEN. Non-negotiables: shown BEFORE the camera activates; a SEPARATE unticked affirmative control, NOT bundled into the ToS or Privacy Policy (bundling is the single most common BIPA failure and the first thing plaintiffs plead); e-signature/tap is sufficient (confirmed by the 2024 BIPA amendment). Copy must state (a) that a BIOMETRIC identifier / face geometry scan is collected and stored — use the word 'biometric', do not soften it to 'photo check'; (b) the specific purpose (identity verification at account opening); (c) the SPECIFIC LENGTH OF TERM as an actual duration, not 'as long as necessary' — Illinois s.15(b)(2) requires the term be stated and vagueness here is a frequently pleaded defect; (d) that it is disclosed to a named third-party verification provider — this is a SEPARATE consent under s.15(d), collection consent is not disclosure consent; (e) how to withdraw consent and what happens if they do.

DELIVERABLE 2 — PUBLIC RETENTION POLICY. Must be written, at a PUBLIC URL (not in-app, not behind login), and LIVE BEFORE the first scan is ever taken — Mora v. J&M Plating means it cannot be drafted retroactively. Must contain a retention schedule, permanent-destruction guidelines, AND a data-security-incident response protocol (Colorado s.6-1-1314 requires the breach protocol; BIPA does not, so Colorado sets the ceiling).

Blocked on: the retain-vs-delete decision, since the stated retention term must match what we actually do.

subtasks.title: Build consent logging that can reproduce any individual user's exact consent screen and timestamp
subtasks.description:
Engineering task, and it is the difference between a defensible case and an indefensible one. If we cannot show, for a named plaintiff, the precise notice text they saw and the moment they accepted, we effectively cannot defend the claim regardless of how good the screen was.

REQUIREMENTS:
- Per-user record: user ID, timestamp, the VERSION IDENTIFIER of the notice text displayed, the consent artifact, and separately the vendor-disclosure consent (BIPA s.15(d) is a distinct violation from s.15(b)).
- Version and archive every version of the notice copy INDEFINITELY. Illinois has a 5-year lookback on notice/consent claims, so a screen retired years ago still has to be reproducible.
- Store the consent record SEPARATELY from the biometric data so that deleting the faceprint does not delete the proof of consent.
- *** RETENTION CONFLICT TO GET RIGHT: the biometric data should be deleted within 24-48h, but California's ARL requires proof of subscription consent be kept for a MINIMUM of 3 years, or 1 year post-termination, whichever is longer. Two different records, two different retention rules, two different stores. Do not let 'delete the signup record' wipe the ARL evidence, and do not let 'keep consent proof for 3 years' become a reason to retain the faceprint. This is the most likely place for the biometric and subscription workstreams to collide destructively. ***
- Implement the deletion job itself with logging, so we can prove destruction actually happened and when.

subtasks.title: Fix the IDV vendor contract: no training, deletion flow-through, audit right, DPA
subtasks.description:
Our own compliance does not discharge us, and the vendor's does not either — Davis v. Jumio and Rivera/McGoveran v. AWS confirm BOTH the app and the vendor can be liable, and Amazon's 'we did everything we could to comply' argument was rejected on the merits. Get these into the contract before launch.

CHECKLIST:
1. STRIKE any licence permitting use of our users' biometric data to train, improve, benchmark or develop models or services. This is the current litigation frontier — 2026 BIPA cases are targeting biometric extraction for AI training as a new route to class-wide claims, and Texas has brought CUBI actions over AI training on biometric identifiers since 2022. Vendor 'service improvement' clauses are the usual hiding place.
2. DELETION FLOW-THROUGH: vendor must delete the template and source image on the same clock we do, with written confirmation and an AUDIT RIGHT. Their retention is our liability.
3. VERIFY any 'zero-data' or 'ephemeral matching' architecture claim TECHNICALLY AND CONTRACTUALLY. Vendors market this precisely because it shrinks legal surface, but a marketing page is not a defence. Get it warranted.
4. NO SALE / NO PROFIT warranty — flat prohibition in IL/TX/WA/CO/NYC that consent cannot cure.
5. CCPA service-provider / contractor terms binding them to our specified business purposes only (required if/when we are CCPA-covered).
6. Security: encryption in transit and at rest; Texas's standard is care at least as protective as how they treat their own confidential information.
7. Indemnity for biometric privacy claims, and check whether their cap is a realistic multiple of BIPA class exposure. Most vendor caps are not.
8. Confirm which entity is the 'collector' in their architecture — it affects who owes the s.15(b) notice, though realistically we owe it regardless.

subtasks.title: Re-verify current status of the Texas/Utah/Louisiana App Store Accountability Acts
subtasks.description:
TIME-SENSITIVE AND EXPLICITLY STALE — do not rely on my findings here without re-checking. These impose duties on APP DEVELOPERS, not just app stores, and a general-audience consumer app is in scope.

WHAT I ESTABLISHED: Texas SB 2420 took effect 1 Jan 2026 after the Fifth Circuit STAYED a preliminary injunction in Nov 2025. Utah (March 2025) and Louisiana HB 570 (30 June 2025) have their own versions. Developer duties include receiving and confirming app-store-supplied age and parental-consent signals, using them only for compliance, transmitting them with industry-standard encryption, and DELETING them after use (Texas). There is limited good-faith protection for relying on app-store data but NO broad safe harbour for our own implementation errors.

WHY RE-CHECK: practitioner trackers note the enforcement timelines and liability frameworks for all three shifted during 2026 due to later legislation and court rulings, and there is a June 2026 status update. Constitutional challenges are live. Confirm what is actually in force NOW, then determine what our app must implement.

START HERE: Wiley's ASAA alert (https://www.wiley.law/alert-State-App-Store-Accountability-Acts-Introduce-New-Obligations-for-App-Developers) which carries the June 2026 update, and the Morrison Foerster piece on the Fifth Circuit stay.

subtasks.title: Build the subscription auto-renewal flow to the California ARL standard
subtasks.description:
Separate workstream from biometrics, same launch date, and for a consumer subscription app this is a HIGHER-probability claim than a biometric one in most states.

CRITICAL CONTEXT — MUCH ONLINE ADVICE IS NOW WRONG: the FTC's 'click-to-cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED IN FULL by the Eighth Circuit on 8 July 2025 (Custom Communications v. FTC), on procedural grounds, days before its main provisions were due to bite. Check the date on any checklist you're handed. What survives and still binds us: ROSCA, FTC Act s.5, state UDAP laws, and all state auto-renewal statutes. The FTC has restarted the rulemaking under Magnuson-Moss procedures, so a replacement is likely — build to click-to-cancel anyway.

BUILD TO CALIFORNIA'S ARL as amended by AB 2863 (amendments effective 1 July 2025), which is the strictest:
- FREE TRIALS ARE COVERED. 'Free-to-pay conversion' is now within 'automatic renewal' and 'continuous service.' If we run a trial, it is in scope.
- Affirmative consent to the auto-renewal terms, separate from consent to everything else. No dark patterns. Do NOT treat confirming billing information as consent.
- RETAIN PROOF OF CONSENT for at least 3 years, or 1 year after termination, whichever is longer. See the consent-logging subtask — this record must be stored separately from the biometric data, which is on a much shorter deletion clock.
- ANNUAL REMINDER to each subscriber: renewal frequency, amount charged, clear cancellation instructions.
- CANCELLATION in the same channel used to sign up, plus a click-to-cancel button for online signups. No obstruction or delay.
Enforced by the CA AG and district attorneys, and a standard hook for UCL class actions.

subtasks.title: Write the data protection assessment / risk assessment document for the face scan
subtasks.description:
A required written deliverable that is very commonly skipped, and it is the first thing a regulator asks for. One document can satisfy most states.

WHY REQUIRED:
- Every Tier 2 comprehensive-privacy-law state requires a DATA PROTECTION ASSESSMENT for processing sensitive data, and biometric data is sensitive data in all of them. Applies once we cross each state's thresholds.
- CALIFORNIA, if in scope: 11 CCR s.7150(a) requires a RISK ASSESSMENT COMPLETED BEFORE initiating processing that involves 'significant risk,' and 'processing sensitive personal information' is an express trigger. In effect since 1 Jan 2026. Either the CPPA or the AG can demand a copy at any time and we must produce it within 30 DAYS. Note: submission of assessments to the CPPA and ADMT pre-use notice duties phase in from April 2027 / Dec 2027; cybersecurity audits phase from April 2028 to April 2030 by revenue band.
- MARYLAND MODPA needs something extra and specific: a documented NECESSITY ASSESSMENT. MODPA BANS collecting or processing sensitive data unless STRICTLY NECESSARY to provide the product or service the consumer requested, and CONSENT DOES NOT CURE IT. We must be able to show identity verification at signup is strictly necessary. MODPA also treats biometric data as sensitive regardless of how it's used, unlike most states.

COVER: purpose and necessity of the face scan, data flows including the vendor, the retention and deletion schedule, security controls, risks to consumers and mitigations, alternatives considered and why rejected (this is where the necessity argument lives), and the minors analysis.

ALSO NOTE, and get counsel's view: CCPA ADMT pre-use-notice and opt-out duties attach to automated decisions that are 'significant decisions' — a concept aimed at lending, housing, employment, healthcare and education. Access to a consumer subscription app is probably NOT a significant decision, so ADMT duties likely do not apply, but a failed face match does deny service, so confirm rather than assume.

subtasks.title: Set a recurring quarterly review of state-law thresholds against actual user counts
subtasks.description:
Ongoing, not a launch task, but it will be forgotten if it isn't a task. Most Tier 2 obligations are DORMANT at launch and switch on silently as we grow. Nobody gets a notification.

WHAT TO CHECK EACH QUARTER:
1. Per-state user counts against each state's threshold. Common trigger is 100,000 state residents. Specific ones to watch: RHODE ISLAND is unusually low at 35,000 and has NO cure period; CALIFORNIA triggers at >$26,625,000 revenue for the 2026 compliance year (inflation-adjusted annually — recheck the figure), or 100,000+ CA consumers, or 50%+ of revenue from selling/sharing PI.
2. Whether we still qualify as an SBA small business. This is the ONLY thing keeping us out of the TEXAS TDPSA and the NEBRASKA law, both of which have NO revenue or volume threshold otherwise. Broadly <500 employees or under ~$7M average receipts, but it is industry-specific by NAICS code. Losing this status is a step change in obligations, not a gradual one.
3. Whether Arkansas's 60-day APDPA cure period has expired (it ends 1 Jan 2027).
4. NEW YORK — the highest-impact watch item. A BIPA-clone bill (S1422, Sen. Liu) creating a private right of action has been introduced and is still pending. If NY enacts it, our risk map changes overnight and NY is a far bigger market than Illinois. Note NY's Health Information Privacy Act did not advance.
5. Any newly enacted state biometric statute. No new dedicated biometric law passed in 2025 and Arkansas stripped the biometric provisions out of SB 258, so the Tier 1 list (IL, TX, WA, CO) has been stable — but this is the thing that would most change the analysis.

USEFUL TRACKER: BCLP's US biometric laws and pending legislation tracker, updated periodically: https://www.bclplaw.com/en-US/events-insights-news/us-biometric-laws-and-pending-legislation-tracker.html

NOTE: Colorado is deliberately NOT on this checklist — its biometric duties have NO threshold and apply from the first Colorado user, so it is a launch obligation, not a scaling one.
